title: Night of the Ninjas

lines.text: This audio program is presented by audible.com.
Audible. Audio that speaks to you wherever you are.
Jack and Annie were walking home from the library.
The path went right by the Frog Creek woods.
“Then you don’t have to come,” said Annie.
She took off into the woods.
But Annie had disappeared among the trees.
He was starting to lose hope.
Maybe he would never see Morgan again.
And there had not been one sign of Morgan le Fay.
Nor had there been one sign of her magic tree house.
Oh, she’s just pretending as usual, Jack thought.
But his heart started to race.
“She better not be kidding,” said Jack.
He took off into the woods to find Annie.
It was hard to see through the shadows.
Annie waved from the window of a tree house.
It was in the tallest oak in the woods.
A long rope ladder hung down from it.
The magic tree house was back.
Jack ran to the rope ladder.
He climbed and climbed and climbed.
As he climbed, he looked out over the woods.
High above the treetops it was still light.
At last, Jack pulled himself into the tree house.
On the floor the letter M glowed in the dim light.
The M stood for Morgan le Fay.
But there was no sign of Morgan herself.
“I wonder where Morgan is,” said Jack.
“Maybe she went to the library to get some more books,” said Annie.
We would have seen her,” said Jack.
A little mouse ran out from behind a stack of books.
It ran to the M shining in the floor.
The mouse sat on the middle of the M.
It looked up at Jack and Annie.
Jack had to admit the mouse was cute.
It had brownand-white fur and big dark eyes.
Annie slowly reached out her hand.
“Just because the mouse is in the tree house doesn’t mean it’s magic.
It’s a plain old mouse that crawled in, that’s all.”
He saw a piece of paper on the floor.
Jack went over and picked up the paper.
“Oh man,” whispered Jack, after he read the words.
I think she’s in big trouble!”
Jack showed Annie the piece of paper.
“Maybe she was trying to write things,” said Jack.
“See how the n sort of runs off the page?”
“Maybe the spell was starting to make her disappear or something,” said Annie.
“I wonder if she left any other clues.”
He glanced around the tree house.
Annie pointed at a book in the corner.
“That’s the only open book,” she said.
He felt a shiver go down his spine.
Jack went over to the book and picked it up.
He held it near the window.
Light from the setting sun was golden on the page.
Jack stared at the picture on it.
In the picture were trees with white flowers.
The trees were on the side of a mountain.
Two people were also in the picture.
They had black scarves over their faces.
And long swords strapped to their backs.
“Morgan must have left the book open to this page for a reason,” said Jack.
“Maybe that’s where she was when the spell got her,” Annie said.
“Or maybe that’s where the four things are,” said Jack.
“But we should read this book first,” said Jack.
She grabbed the book from Jack.
“We have to find out about this place.”
Annie held the book out of reach.
“We’ll find out when we get there,” she said.
“We don’t even know where there is!”
But Annie pointed at the picture.
“I wish we could go here,” she said.
The leaves of the oak tree began to shake.
Then she put it in the pouch of her sweatshirt.
The tree house started to spin.
Except for the sound of rushing water.
Annie was already looking out the window.
The mouse peeked out of her pouch.
Jack looked out the window, too.
The air was fresh and cool.
The tree house was in a tree with white flowers.
The tree was in a grove of trees on the side of a mountain.
Nearby a wild stream rushed downhill.
Two ninjas were standing on rocks near the water.
They were staring at the valley below.
They wore black pants and shirts.
They had black scarves around their heads.
And swords strapped to their backs.
It was exactly like the picture in the book.
“They might think we’re some kind of enemy,” said Jack quietly.
Jack pushed his glasses into place.
Now he was going to look at the ninja book.
He read: Very little is known about the shadowy warriors called ninjas.
Historians believe that ninjas lived in Japan between the 14th and 17th centuries.
Both men and women were ninjas.
Sometimes they fought to protect their families.
Sometimes warlords hired them to be spies.
“We’re in Japan, hundreds of years ago.”
He pulled out his notebook and pencil.
I think they know we’re here.”
His eyes met the dark eyes of the tall ninja.
He and Annie looked around wildly.
But where was the book about Pennsylvania?
It had the picture of the Frog Creek woods in it.
Jack and Annie couldn’t get home without it.
He and Annie grabbed the top of the rope ladder.
They pulled the ladder into the tree house.
But the tall ninja leaped at the tree trunk.
Then he started climbing up the tree!
Jack and Annie huddled in a corner.
The ninjas climbed into the tree house.
The ninjas pulled iron bands off their hands.
The bands had spikes like claws on them.
“That’s how they climbed the tree,” Annie whispered to Jack.
The ninjas stared at Jack and Annie with dark, piercing eyes.
The rest of their faces were covered by their scarves.
Jack felt frozen under their stares.
She stepped right up to them.
They were as still as Jack.
“We’re trying to help our friend, Morgan,” said Annie.
The tall ninja took the note from her.
Then he gave it to the short ninja.
The two ninjas stared at each other.
Then they looked back at Jack and Annie.
Finally the short ninja nodded once.
He put the note into the pocket of his shirt.
Jack wished he could see their faces.
He couldn’t tell what they were thinking.
The short ninja tossed the rope ladder back out of the tree house.
The tall one pointed down the ladder.
Then he pointed at Jack and Annie.
The short ninja darted down the ladder.
His feet didn’t touch the rungs of the ladder.
The tall one did the same.
They were like spiders dropping from webs.
“Now’s our chance to leave,” said Jack.
He looked around the tree house again.
“Let’s go with them, Jack,” said Annie.
“But I think they know something about Morgan!”
Jack put his notebook and the ninja book into his pack.
He pushed his glasses into place.
And he started down the ladder.
Jack joined Annie and the ninjas on the ground.
The sun had fallen behind the hills.
The sky was streaked with red and gold.
The mouse peeked out from Annie’s sweatshirt pouch.
But who is going to take care of us?
The short ninja held Jack’s arm in one hand and Annie’s arm in the other.
He led them through the twilight.
The tall ninja walked behind them.
The ninjas stopped near the rushing water of the wide stream.
The water roared as it raced downhill.
The short ninja looked at Jack and Annie.
He let go of their arms.
Then he pushed them toward the stream.
Then he and the short ninja stepped into the wild stream.
“Let’s run back to the tree house!”
"Let's run back to the treehouse," said Jack.
Together they stepped into the water.
They both screamed and jumped out.
It was the coldest water Jack had ever felt!
It was so cold it felt like fire.
“I can’t go back in,” said Annie, shivering.
The ninjas looked at Jack and Annie.
Then they turned around and came back.
But the ninja lifted Jack high into the air.
And put him on his shoulder.
The short ninja put Annie on his shoulder.
Then the two ninjas stepped into the stream again.
The icy wild waters swirled around them.
It went up to the short ninja’s waist.
But the ninjas moved through the stream as calmly as two sailing ships.
Then they were on dry land.
The ninjas lowered Jack and Annie to the ground.
The ninjas said nothing, but they looked around.
A full moon was rising in the sky.
Dark rocks dotted the side of the mountain.
They went silently up the slope, between the rocks.
Jack wasn’t afraid of the ninjas now.
In fact, he was starting to like them.
Maybe they really could help find Morgan.
But Jack and Annie made plenty of noise.
They panted as they climbed the rocky hillside.
Their wet sneakers made squishy sounds.
Jack could see their eyes darting around.
Voices were coming from the valley below.
Jack saw torches flaming in the mist.
Jack and Annie hurried after them.
Jack was too out of breath to speak.
He also didn’t have an answer.
They came to a pine forest.
The ninjas moved like ghosts through the forest.
They appeared and disappeared, through moonlight and shadows.
Jack and Annie struggled to keep up.
Finally the ninjas came to a stop.
One ninja held out his hand, as if to say, Wait.
Then both ninjas stepped away into the shadows of the trees.
He pulled the ninja book out of his pack.
He turned the pages until he came to a picture of a cave.
By the light of the full moon, he read: Sometimes ninjas held meetings in hidden mountain caves to plan secret missions.
“Oh man,” said Jack, “I bet they went inside a hidden cave.”
He pulled out his notebook and pencil.
He wrote: Jack turned the page.
He stared at a picture of a ninja sitting on a mat.
He read: Ninjas took orders from a ninja master.
The master was a mysterious wise person who knew many secrets of nature.
Just then the two ninjas returned.
Jack quickly put his books away.
The short ninja motioned for Jack and Annie to follow.
In the shadows was the entrance of a dark cave.
Jack and Annie went into the cave.
They followed the ninja through the darkness.
The back of the cave was lit with dozens of candles.
In the flickering light, Jack saw a dark figure sitting on a woven mat.
The ninja bowed to the master.
Then he stepped to one side.
The master stared at Jack and Annie.
Jack and Annie sat on the cold, hard floor.
The mouse poked its head out of Annie’s pouch.
The master stared at the mouse for a moment.
“I’m Jack and that’s my sister, Annie,” Jack answered.
“We’re trying to help our friend Morgan le Fay,” said Jack.
Annie pointed to the short ninja.
“You mean, you gave the message to her,” said the ninja master.
“And she has given it to me.”
Jack thought she might be smiling.
The master held up Morgan’s note.
“Perhaps I can help you,” he said.
“But first you must prove yourselves worthy of my help.”
Just then the tall ninja appeared.
He made a sign to the master.
He handed Morgan’s note to Annie.
He knew that the samurai were fierce Japanese fighters.
“Were they the ones in the valley?”
“Yes, our family is at war with them,” said the master.
“We must leave before they find us.”
The master strapped on his sword.
“I have no time now,” he said.
“No, there is no place for you where we are going.
You must find your way back to your house in the trees.”
“They will think you are one of us,” said the master.
They will show you no mercy.”
“But you have seen the way of the ninja.
You can practice it yourselves now,” said the master.
“Your tree house lies to the east.
That is the way you must go,” he said.
How do we find the east?
Before he could ask, the master bowed.
Then he disappeared into the shadows.
The two ninjas led Jack and Annie out of the cave, into the moonlight.
The tall one pointed at the pine forest.
Then they too disappeared into the darkness.
Jack and Annie were all alone.
Jack and Annie stood still for a long moment.
“Well, I guess the tall ninja was pointing to the east,” she said.
“I guess that’s the way we go.”
“I need to write some stuff down.”
In the moonlight, he wrote: Look, Jack,” whispered Annie.
She had pulled her sweatshirt hood over her head and tied the strings tightly.
She did look like a ninja—a very small one.
He pulled his hood up, too.
Then he and Annie headed east into the woods.
All the trees looked the same.
Were they still going in the right direction?
They both stared at the woods around them.
“Do you think we’re still going east?”
Just then the master’s words came back to Jack.
“The ninja master said to use nature,” he said.
“Wait, I remember something—” Jack closed his eyes.
He remembered something in a camping book.
First we need a stick,” he said.
“Great, now we just need a space with moonlight,” said Jack.
They moved into a moonlit space between the shadows.
“Now push the stick into the ground,” Jack said.
Annie pushed the stick into the ground.
“The stick’s shadow looks like it’s more than six inches,” said Jack.
Then that means the shadow’s pointing east,” said Jack.
Jack pointed to a new direction.
They took off—heading east, they hoped.
Soon they were out of the pine woods and walking down the rocky mountainside.
They moved slowly from rock to rock.
Finally they rested against a giant rock.
“Let’s check our direction again,” said Jack.
Annie stuck another stick into the dirt.
He pointed to the shadow on the ground.
“That way—” Annie peeked over the rock, down the mountain.
There were flames of fire coming up the mountain.
Jack and Annie ducked behind the rock.
He pulled out the ninja book.
“I hope something in here can help us,” he said.
Jack flipped through page after page until he found what he was looking for.
It was a picture of warriors wearing bamboo armor.
He read: The samurai were fierce Japanese fighters.
They carried two swords to cut down their enemies.
Annie tapped Jack on the shoulder.
A figure was coming down toward them.
In the moonlight, his bamboo armor was shining.
Samurai were on both sides of them now.
The warrior stepped closer and closer.
But he squeezed his eyes shut.
Then he tried to be part of the rock.
Jack tried to be as still as the rock.
Soon he started feeling as strong as the rock.
He wanted to be the rock forever.
Jack stood up and looked over the rock.
He felt great—he was getting more and more like a ninja every minute.
Maybe even like a ninja master.
Down the mountain, between the rocks.
Until they came to the wide, icy stream.
The water seemed even wilder than before.
“I don’t see the tree house,” said Annie.
Jack looked across the stream to the dark grove of trees.
Moonlight shone on their pale flowers.
But where was the tree house?
“I don’t see it either,” said Jack.
“We have to cross the water first.
Then we’ll try and find it.”
The water was crashing and rushing over the rocks.
The mouse peeked out from its pouch.
She patted the mouse’s little head.
He took a deep breath and stepped into the stream.
The icy water swirled up to his knees.
He held on tight as water swirled around him.
She helped him back onto the bank.
Luckily, they hadn’t fallen off in the water.
“N-not really,” said Jack, his teeth chattering.
He was chilled to the bone.
He pulled off the hood of his sweatshirt.
He didn’t feel much like a ninja anymore.
Annie pulled off her hood, too.
Peanut climbed out of Annie’s sweatshirt pouch and leaped onto the ground.
“We have to do what the master said!”
In the moonlight Jack saw the little mouse.
It was running through the grass along the stream.
They ran beside the rushing waters.
A moonlit branch had fallen across a narrow part of the stream.
The mouse was running over the branch.
The mouse vanished into the tall grass on the other side of the stream.
Jack and Annie stared at the tree branch.
“We have to try to cross it,” said Annie.
“Maybe if we pretend we’re mice, we can do it,” said Annie.
“If you could be a rock, you can be a mouse,” said Annie.
“Just be teeny and light and fast.”
“It’ll help you feel more like a mouse.”
Then he darted across the branch.
Jack moved so quickly, he didn’t think about anything —except getting to the other side.
He forgot the wild, freezing water.
He forgot the smallness of the branch.
Suddenly Jack was on the other side.
Suddenly Annie was right beside him.
They laughed and fell together into the grass.
“I guess it was big enough,” said Jack.
“I guess we just had to think the right way.”
He was still wet from his fall into the stream.
Jack pushed his glasses into place and stood up.
“Okay, now we just have to find the tree house,” he said.
The tree house was outlined against the moonlit sky.
In the distance came the sound of voices.
“The samurai are coming back,” said Jack.
The voices of the samurai were getting closer.
He pulled her toward the rope ladder.
Annie started up the rope ladder.
He liked that little mouse now.
Just before they got to the top, Jack heard it.
Annie pulled herself into the tree house.
Someone else was in the tree house, too.
A dark figure was sitting in the corner.
“You have done well,” the figure said.
“You have followed the way of the ninja,” he said.
“Take good care of your little helper,” he said, handing the mouse to Annie.
Annie kissed the mouse’s tiny head.
He held his hand out to Jack.
He gave Jack a small, round stone.
“This moonstone will help you find your missing friend,” the master said.
Was this one of the four things?
“You must go home now,” said the master.
He picked up the Pennsylvania book and handed it to Annie.
Because your heart knew you had a mission to complete first.”
There will be more help along the way.
But you must find the way on your own.”
She found the picture of Frog Creek.
“I wish we could go there,” she said.
The white flowers started to shake.
“Remember,” the master said, “keep a kind heart.”
Then he swung silently down the rope ladder.
He disappeared into the dark night.
There was so much he wanted to ask the master.
But the tree house started to spin.
Jack gripped the stone in his hand.
He stared at the moonstone in his hand.
Annie and the mouse were looking out the window.
The sun was setting in the distance.
No time at all had passed in Frog Creek.
They heard their neighbor’s dog, Henry, bark.
In the distance, they could see their dad step out of their house.
Jack sat back on his heels.
He looked at the moonstone again.
“I guess we have one of the four things,” he said.
“We’ll look for the other three tomorrow,” Annie said.
They had a lot more work to do.
He put the moonstone in his pocket.
She took off one of her sneakers.
Then she put her sneaker back on.
You know, for Peanut to sleep in.”
She tucked it inside her sock.
Annie held the mouse close to Jack.
“Thanks for helping us,” Annie said to the mouse.
She put Peanut gently down on the glowing M.
She pulled Morgan’s message out of her pouch.
And put it next to the mouse.
Then she started down the ladder.
For a moment, its dark eyes looked old and wise.
Then Jack headed down the rope ladder.
It got darker and darker as he went down.
By the time he stepped onto the ground, it was almost completely black.
Together they took off through the cool, dark woods.
They moved silently and swiftly—two shadow warriors returning home.
